title: Spelling of jass, fights at dances, and the Newport Festival
summary: Jazz as low-class music, fighting at dances, and trips to New York.

bands.name: Zulu Social Aid and Pleasure Club

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Because the people have the fine musicians playing just like us. And they have albums or jazz that they give you that they record and you perceive for yourself and you hear them playing. You see how they are. That's what we gave to the world, United States. Especially in the already jazz. Do you know how jazz was supposed to spell? J-A-S-S. Right? They used to have an old drummer at the Hall. I don't know if it's still got it. That's where it really fell. But it got so offensive because you saw it put the Z behind it. See, here you always had a certain class of people that didn't appreciate this kind of music way back then. They called it low down. Low class of music people, white and black.
Well, it was at least a lot of people associated with the whorehouses.

I don't know if it was a little bit of a dance. I don't know if I said it was low class. Well, this is what I want to tell you. When I was with the Pensacola Jazz Band, it's two places. It's a place, at that time when you went to Florida, you went to Mobile on a train. And then they had a boat for the train to cross. You know, I forgot where it was. And right there where they had a band from y'all, a white band. And we were on the train. We was on the train. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. The train stopped. After you leave there, the train stopped. Some other person before you get to Pensacola. I called them hillbillers. And this Pensacola band, I'm not sure if I'm sure they hired us to play for them. And in Mobile, the Rack Orchers wouldn't let some of these people come in like the boss of the group, you know. And on the outskirt of Mobile somewhere, they hired us. And we knew what to expect. The people would have to get that moonshine in them, they're going to get to fight and so on and so on and so on. So that man had a man with a gun by us. And we were a group. And on the outskirt of Mobile, they had a man with a gun by us. And the gun by us would fight but they didn't get on that bandstand. And you had the Italian Hall and Esplanade. We'd play for them. Boites, marriage, things like that. And they would fight. We played in the Irish Channel. Talking about it before, even before I went to Pensacola. We would fight. But then white people would protect us. We'd fight among the suburbs.
We'd have to make sure they were on the front.

We'd have a police stand and everything. Well, the police were standing around the bandstand? I'm saying this because all that's pertaining to jazz, how people respect you if you carry yourself in the right place. Of course, there was some black guys themselves because they were doing things they weren't supposed to. They knew better. I'd do that myself. Somebody don't take advantage of me or take something that belongs to me. You understand? Yeah. I was used to find out. It was like Mr. Cohen. Way back then, if you want to live in Chicago and things like that, I would be second honk with his guys. I'd know if he followed the tune or the parades or the bulls for love or the Zulus and things like that. And I wish to tell myself, I'm lucky when I should come. I'm kind of scared myself. I'm worried about that. So far, I never heard nothing happen to him. No? Nothing happened to him.
Just a few pickpockets, that's all. Nothing serious?

No, well, I'm talking about getting injured. Yeah. Right now and today, my wife and I'm hired, we stay right here. I don't go nowhere. We just do things. It's a pretty fair neighborhood. I mean, my wife and all those things like that. I mean, when she was there, I mean, if she wanted to go, she went a lot of places to me. You know, years past, but years changed the thing. I took a trip to her. We used to have that trip going to New York for Newport Festival. I took her on one there and she really enjoyed herself. I got on these paper clippings. We played on the boat. It's a Staten Island boat. And they had that white band, what they call it, the World Greatest Jazz Band. It was two times we played against her. I'm not saying for a race to pressure, but you know, we had more people be on where we played than they would. Because I'd go up there and see them. And she met some people she knew from New York. And they took a picture over and they had it in the paper the next day. And they had a brother of priests. And they lived up there at that time. And all those big powerful bands. And we had a trip with Kit Thomas. Concert tour. We went to, we went to, what was it? Oh, sure.
